I had a very scary experience with the new model 3 last weekend. I got an extended test drive during the whole weekend, so I tested it vigorously. I found myself constantly looking down before pressing the turn signal buttons before exiting roundabouts, particularly the smaller ones. Otherwise, it's impossible to hit the correct button, and even then it's too easy to hit the wrong one. I found that I lost track of my surroundings and became way too distracted at times because of this. 
One time I almost hit a pedestrian when exiting a roundabout. I was too focused on finding the button to press. I only looked down for a few seconds, but that was enough. When I looked up, a pedestrian was suddenly right in front of me and I had to slam on the brakes. Other cars behind me had to do the same and nearly hit me from behind. That really scared me. I've been driving for 20 years, and I've never been close to running over anyone before. I think these buttons are dangerous and shouldn't be legal. it's the only thing keeping me from buying one. I loved so many of the upgrades, so this was a real shame. I really liked the car, but I'm not sure I would ever be comfortable using this.
I live in the EU by the way, and we have roundabouts everywhere. It's probably not much of an issue in the US though.

text:
For everyone looking forward for a refreshed Model 3 Performance. Possibly called “Model 3 Ludicrous”

Now we know Musk has said that he won’t do a Plaid Model 3 because it would “complicate” the Model 3.

I believe that what he means by this is that putting two Plaid motors in the rear would require so many design changes that it wouldn’t be worth it. However, that doesn’t mean a Model 3 couldn’t get extremely fast with just two motors.

Just look at the trap speeds of a refreshed Model S LR. They are hitting 130+ mph in the 1/4 mile but they really aren’t that much quicker in the 1/4 mile because their 60 foot times are even slower than a Model 3 Performance.

However, if you go back to older Model S Ludicrous cars you can see that those cars could hit sub 1.6 60’ times but they were only trapping about 4 mph more than my Model 3 Performance with weight reductions.

The key here is if you simply combined the top end pulling power of the current Model S LR with the launch modes of the older Model S cars and put it in a Model 3 you would get ridiculous times with almost no complexity added to the Model 3.

The Model 3 doesn’t need three motors to be fast. It doesn’t even need Plaid Carbon wrapped motors to be fast.

It just needs to be able to do a proper launch and be able to hold max power at higher speeds.

If we could turn a 1.60 60’ with a 128+ mph trap speed the Model 3 Ludicrous would probably be able to keep up with a the Corvette E-Ray(10.4) in the 1/4 mile.

I honestly think they might be able to do that with the current 82.1 KWh battery and the two Model S LR motors.

Some of the P90D cars could hit 2.8 second true 0-60 mph times without subtracting rollout. They were hitting plenty of power with less than 10% more battery power than the current Model 3 Performance has.

The current battery is capable of producing plenty of power. You just need motors that can take that power at much higher speeds.

If they do a Model 3 Ludicrous this year I actually think it will be quicker than people are expecting but it won’t have a vastly different batttery or even vastly different motors. I think 10.4 @ 128+ mph is possible and possibly even 0-60 mph in 2.5 seconds. 

As of right now, The absolute quickest acceleration in the Model 3 Performance is achieved when the battery pack temperature is between 125 to 137 degrees Fahrenheit, the State of Charge is 100%, and the motors are as cold as possible. That will give you a “Max Discharge Value” of 629 HP or 462 KW at the battery.

A Model 3 Performance would probably dyno at 538-545 WHP if it was new and fully optimized.

Let us know what kind of times you are expecting if they produce a Tesla Model 3 Ludicrous.

*Notes/Info from Travis Wills*

The car had already been attacked by rust after one winter. This is due to a total lack of rust protection, mixed materials and a far too thin layer of paint.

Now the Danish FDM, the equivalent of the Motormen in Sweden, has gone through the warranty regulations for the most common car brands, where, among other things, rust protection and warranty are one of the parameters.

In the report, which was presented in March 2023, FDM notes that Tesla's warranty is deficient in some respects.

On the one hand, it does not cover all the mechanics connected to the electric drive, which FDM considers to be a consumer requirement. The charging cable, the high current connector and the batteries do not have full warranty coverage.

However, it is the rust protection guarantee that is the worst.

It does not cover paint damage or rust damage, which does not come from the inside.

The warranty terms state: “The Limited Lifetime Body Repair Warranty covers repairs resulting from pitting and deterioration of body parts, but excludes damage caused by rust”.

Just rust through
We Car owners have also noted Tesla's flawed rust protection warranty, which only applies to rusting through, and asked rust protection specialist Thomas Widström about what rusting through means:

“It is extremely rare. It is basically completely impossible for a car owner to prove where the rust has come from," says Thomas Widström.

For those of you who are thinking of giving your Tesla your own good rust protection, however, also have to think twice. This is what it says in the rust protection guarantee:

"Corrosion and paint defects caused due to or as a result of accidents, paint treatment, abuse, negligence, improper maintenance or operation of the vehicle, installation of an accessory, exposure to chemical substances."
The warranty expires
If you treat the undercarriage of your Tesla yourself, it counts as "exposure to chemical substances" and the rust protection then ceases to apply.

This is where Tesla differs from the crowd.

Most other car brands accept that the car owner himself supplements with paint and anti-rust treatments. But in Tesla's case, the warranty then ceases to apply.

Norwegian rust company Funderud Antirust took apart a Model Y to examine the car. According to the film, the rust protection of the best-selling electric car has major flaws, despite a 12-year rust protection guarantee against rusting through. Among other things, exposed areas are not covered by inner screens, the chassis is not galvanized and there is no undercarriage treatment at all. The paintwork is also considerably thinner than on most other cars. Where steel and aluminum meet, galvanic corrosion can also occur.
- We see that there is no PVC wear coating in either the spring tower or the chassis. And we notice the sheet metal joints here. There is no seal in the joints of the plate, which means that salt and water can seep in between.

The Audi is awkward. You step on the gas pedal, and you wait a second as it feels like it's bogged down, then without warning, the turbo kicks in for angry acceleration, even if you don't want it. In the most "dynamic" setting, the car is numb, and it reminds me of my 1981 Buick Regal I had in high school. You'll never upset the chassis in the Audi because it's so underpowered. And, it's no fun to drive. 

To add insult: I can't figure out how to refuel the Audi from my house. I have to stop at gas stations. 

I can't wait to get my 2019 Model 3 back from the shop...

⭐⭐⭐ EXECUTIVE SUMMARY ⭐⭐⭐
The 2026 Tesla Model 3 Standard is positioned as the cheapest car in Tesla's lineup, saving buyers over $5,000 compared to the Premium model. Despite a simpler suspension and a smaller battery, the vehicle retains its core driving dynamics, premium interior feel, and essential features like the panoramic glass roof. The reviewer concludes that the minimal compromises make the Standard model the default, logical choice for most buyers.

⭐⭐⭐ DETAILED BREAKDOWN ⭐⭐⭐
The video provides a comprehensive first drive review of the 2026 Tesla Model 3 Standard, the most affordable vehicle in Tesla's current lineup, priced around $38,630. Presenter Alistair Weaver questions whether this cheaper model suffers from aggressive cost-cutting, similar to what Edmunds observed in the Model Y Standard. 

Starting with the exterior and interior, the changes are minimal. The car features new aerodynamic wheel covers and subtle interior material swaps, like fabric replacing some vegan leather. Crucially, unlike the Model Y, the Model 3 Standard retains the panoramic glass roof and double-glazed front windows. While the rear infotainment screen has been removed—a change the presenter actually praises for family use—the cabin remains comfortable, well-appointed, and avoids feeling like a 'poverty spec' vehicle.

On the road, the Model 3 Standard features a less sophisticated suspension setup compared to the Premium model. However, because the sedan sits lower to the ground than an SUV, body roll is easily managed, resulting in a drive that still feels sporty, responsive, and traditionally Tesla. The smaller battery pack slightly reduces acceleration and range (claiming 321 miles), but the real-world performance remains punchy and more than adequate for daily driving.

Finally, the review touches on Tesla's autonomous driving software. A notable downgrade is that the standard Autopilot in this trim will no longer auto-steer on the highway unless the driver pays for the Full Self-Driving (FSD) upgrade—a move Weaver criticizes as a cynical marketing tactic. Despite this, the overall verdict is highly positive, declaring the Model 3 Standard as the smartest buy in the lineup and a formidable competitor against rivals like the Hyundai Ioniq 6 and Chevy Equinox EV.

⭐⭐⭐ KEY TAKEAWAYS ⭐⭐⭐
🎯 The Model 3 Standard retains premium features like the panoramic glass roof and front double-glazed windows, unlike the heavily de-contented Model Y Standard.
🎯 Despite a simpler suspension, the car's low center of gravity ensures it remains sporty, engaging, and limits body roll.
🎯 The rear infotainment screen has been removed and replaced with physical air vents and USB-C chargers.
🎯 Standard Autopilot on this model is software-limited and will not automatically steer on the highway unless the driver purchases the FSD upgrade.
🎯 At roughly $38,630, the minimal compromises make this trim the best value and default choice for most Model 3 buyers.

⭐⭐⭐ ACTIONABLE ADVICE ⭐⭐⭐
💡 Opt for the Model 3 Standard over the Premium version if you want to save $5,000 and do not require maximum range or track-level performance.
💡 Be aware that to get highway auto-steer functionality, you will need to pay an additional $99/month for the Full Self-Driving software.
💡 Use the frunk (front trunk) for versatile storage, as it remains fully functional and lined, unlike some downgraded models.
